author: Rhonda Clark
text: The first time I called due to a sensor failure, I spoke with someone with an accent other than my own, and he was great.  I was also at first skeptical but quickly got over myself because he answered every question and was super helpful.  Sensor replacement went out the very next day.  (Just to help out a bit more regarding the hearing issues, I also have bad hearing due to a medical issue and had on my bone conduction headphones that anyone can buy, so I could hear clearly out of both ears.  Yes, this actually helps on phone calls.)

author: 匿名互动者 447
text:
You kind of answered your own question. Not being used to your accent pretty much sums it up. It's been going on for years. If you've already struggled dozens of times struggling through a conversation that takes 30 minutes instead of 10, you would understand. Put it this way, if someone throws a rock at you, and you get hit, and it hurts. Why would you want to get hit by a rock again? That person is only protecting themselves from an unpleasant experience. Having an issue where you're dependent on someone else speaking in your own accent is already annoying enough.
Some agents are new and don't know what they're talking about. I'm assuming there are probably quotas and keeping a job can be stressful for everyone. I'm 70 years old and I've been losing my hearing for years. That's sucks all by itself.
You have a job that pays you money. Be grateful in that and that you probably did help someone at some point in your day. And look at all the people that took time out of their day to make you feel better by answering you here. Pass this on to co-workers.
